00:00:00 - The Rivalry Between Ngô Đình Nhu and Ngô Đình Cẩn

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment0

Partial Transcript: Nayan Chanda, whom I think you knew very well.

Segment Synopsis: After a brief discussion about Edward Miller's advisor, professor Hồ Huệ Tâm, PXA discusses the relationship between the Ngô brothers, stating that the perceived rivalry between the intellectual Ngô Đình Nhu and the less-educated Ngô Đình Cẩn was not real. He explains it was an appearance they maintained to gather intelligence on their subordinates. PXA describes Ngô Đình Cẩn as a smart, powerful grassroots operator who worked underground before 1954 to build a constituency in Huế. He states that Cẩn supplied the Diệm regime with key personnel, including men who worked for Nhu, and secretly invested in Buddhist institutions to build influence.

Keywords: Grassroots; Hue; Huế; Hồ Huệ Tâm; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngo Dinh Diem; Ngo Dinh Nhu; Ngo Dinh Thuc; Ngo Family Dynamics; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngô Đình Nhu; Ngô Đình Thục; Rivalry; Ngô Đình Diệm

00:09:50 - Labor Unions

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment590

Partial Transcript: What about Trần Quốc Bửu and the Vietnamese Confederation of Labor?

Segment Synopsis: PXA discusses Trần Quốc Bửu's journey as a politically flexible figure shaped by overlapping foreign influences in Vietnam during the mid-20th century. He initially worked with the Việt Minh and received Japanese training alongside leaders like Nguyễn Bình and Trình Minh Thế. Later, French intelligence recruited him to lead anti-communist labor organizations, countering worker mobilization by communists. In the early 1950s, he cooperated with Ngô Đình Diệm and joined the Cần Lao party under Ngô Đình Nhu’s influence. Despite these alliances with both French and South Vietnamese authorities, his relationship with Diệm’s regime ultimately proved short-lived and unstable.

Keywords: Anti-communism; Catholic Church; Catholic Federation of Workers; French G2; Japanese; Labor Movements in Vietnam; Labor Unions; Ngo Brothers; Tran Quoc Buu; Trần Quốc Bửu

00:14:47 - Dr. Trần Kim Tuyến's Role in 1950s South Vietnamese Politics

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment887

Partial Transcript: 1956, 1955, 1956? Yeah, there was a strike '56.

Segment Synopsis: In 1955–56, Ngô Đình Diệm intensified authoritarian control by abolishing traditional village elections and suppressing opposition, including nationalist and religious groups like the Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo, despite their anti-communist stance. This caused widespread dissatisfaction and strikes, particularly among villagers. At the same time, Dr. Trần Kim Tuyến, a trusted political operative under Ngô Đình Diệm, led the Political, Social, and Cultural Office, which included secret police functions despite his limited formal intelligence training. To prevent communist influence, he deliberately split up the Office as well as made a new labor organization, ensuring mutual surveillance and control. The office had previously been headed by Vũ Tiến Huân, a French-trained administrator and Diệm ally. By late 1956, Tuyến replaced Huân as chief of the Office, following reorganizations. PXA then shifted to discuss Dr. Tuyến's background. He is someone who is more to the Catholic Church than personally to the Ngô family, with a background in religion and literature as well as partial medical education disrupted by French military conscription.

Keywords: 1956; Anti-communism; Catholic; Dr. Tuyen's background; Ngo Dinh Diem; Ngo brothers; Ngô Đình Diệm; Political, Social, and Cultural Office; Tran Kim Tuyen; Vu Tien Huan; Vũ Tiến Huân; political manuevers; Trần Kim Tuyến

00:23:54 - Lê Khắc Duyệt's Role in 1950s South Vietnamese Politics

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment1434

Partial Transcript: Yes. I read about that in, AJ Langguth's book.

Segment Synopsis: The speaker recounts returning from the United States (1957–59) and seeking employment through connections with Lê Khắc Duyệt, the Chief of Police and Security of Central Vietnam under Ngô Đình Cẩn. He describes a period of intense repression in which a large proportion of suspected cadres in Cochinchina were arrested or killed, attributing primary responsibility to Cẩn rather than other officials. These actions allegedly included extralegal detention and transfers to Huế. Duyệt is portrayed as a loyal, due to his French training, non-political administrator who exercised restraint, sometimes delaying harsh orders, and retained Cẩn’s trust despite internal religious and political pressures.

Keywords: Le Khac Duyet; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Lê Khắc Duyệt

00:31:03 - The 1960 Coup Attempt and Ngô Đình Cẩn's Foresight

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment1863

Partial Transcript: But here, they look down upon him in Saigon.

Segment Synopsis: PXA recounts the November 1960 coup attempt and the contempt intellectuals held for Ngô Đình Cẩn despite his foreknowledge. Cẩn sent a detailed warning to Ngô Đình Nhu, who dismissed it due to condescension. This led PXA to meet Cẩn in Huế to understand his intelligence methods. Cẩn used a counterinsurgency strategy involving arresting suspected communist agents, detaining them extralegally, then releasing some as covert informants to monitor nationalist opposition, which is seen as a more immediate threat. This network enabled the regime to track political activity and anticipate coups. Cẩn also commanded respect from subordinates, including Tôn Thất Đính, defending him against the disdain the urban intellectuals had for Cẩn .

Keywords: Anti-communism; Disregard; Dr. Tuyến; Elbridge Durbrow; Intelligence Report; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Ngô Đình Nhu; Ton That Dinh; Tôn Thất Đính; VC; VNQDD; Vietcong; counterinsurgency; intelligence; nationalist opposition; 1960 Coup

00:42:42 - Ngô Đình Cẩn and the Ngô Brothers' Dynamics in the 1950s

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment2562

Partial Transcript: And he was–he seems to have been less Catholic than his brothers,

Segment Synopsis: The passage portrays Ngô Đình Cẩn as a pragmatic operator who built support beyond Catholic networks, unlike some of his family members. It highlights connections between Ngô Đình Thục and international Catholic figures such as Francis Spellman, alongside claims of broader political and intelligence ties with America during the anti-French war. It also suggests coordination rather than rivalry between Cẩn, Ngô Đình Nhu, and Ngô Đình Diệm, using overlapping reporting networks to monitor subordinates. PXA also remarks how Cẩn is smarter than Nhu and Thục due to his ability to discern flatterers.

00:50:46 - The Regime's Decline

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment3046

Partial Transcript: And if that was the case, why did it change after the 1950’s?

Segment Synopsis: PXA discusses why the Diệm regime ultimately failed and the Communist party made a comeback. He states the regime had no real constituency and alienated key segments of the population. He describes how the regime dispossessed peasants of their land through the Agroville and Strategic Hamlet programs, abolished traditional village elections in 1956, and forced Chinese residents to take Vietnamese citizenship, creating widespread animosity. PXA explains that this drove many patriots and intellectuals to support the Việt Minh.

Keywords: Chinese businessmen; Land confiscation; Nationalism; Opposition; Strategic Hamlet; Viet Minh; Vietnamese Rural Politics; Việt Minh; animosity; Agroville

00:58:45 - Bến Cát Intelligence Operation

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment3525

Partial Transcript: So Ngô Ðình Cẩn, I went there. See, I give you some anecdote, many anecdote. He like a cow, with a cow milk.

Segment Synopsis: PXA discusses an intelligence operation run from a dairy farm in Bến Cát. He describes the farm as being run by an Australian air force veteran and established near a communist military zone to recruit local workers and train them as intelligence assets for the South Vietnamese, American, and Australian governments. He also recounts an incident in November 1961 where an Egyptian involved with the farm was kidnapped by local guerrillas, stating the motive was simply to acquire stationery, a typewriter, and paper. Ngô Đình Cẩn’s fondness for animals led subordinates to present gifts like cows and trained dogs from the Bến Cát farm as acts of flattery. PXA highlights how aides exploited minor details to discredit rivals like Phạm Quốc Thuần as well as Cẩn’s role in recruiting loyal personnel, including individuals sent to the United States for training and later integrated into the regime.

Keywords: Australia; Australian Involvement in Vietnam; Ben Cat; CIA; Dairy Farm; Espionage; Intelligence Operations; Kidnapping; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Pham Quoc Thuan; Phạm Quốc Thuần; communists; sycophants; Bến Cát

01:11:24 - The 1963 Buddhist Crisis

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment4284

Partial Transcript: Okay. I'm sure––I think we should probably finish up here because I know you've not been feeling well. Let me ask you one more question, though, about the Buddhist movement in 1963, Phong trào Phật giáo.

Segment Synopsis: PXA describes the 1963 Buddhist movement in Huế as primarily a reaction against Ngô Đình Thục’s religious policies, while noting that Ngô Đình Cẩn initially maintained cooperative relations with Buddhists but followed Thục’s authority in key decisions and aggravations against the Buddhists. He links the unrest to both local grievances, including restrictions on religious expression and the May 1963 Huế incident, and to a longer-term international Buddhist movement for unity. Figures such as Thích Trí Quang are presented as influential organizers, with connections to earlier political and intelligence networks and involvement in protest actions like the self-immolation of Thích Quảng Đức. The account further claims that U.S. actors, including the Central Intelligence Agency, monitored the situation, anticipated unrest, and maintained contacts with Buddhist figures. It also alleges that intelligence files on Trí Quang were destroyed and that he was later positioned in regional Buddhist activities, while journalists and informants were encouraged to closely track Buddhist developments in Huế leading up to the crisis.

Keywords: 1963 Buddhist Crisis; CIA; Catholic Church; Huế; Ngo Dinh Can; Ngo Dinh Thuc; Ngô Đình Cẩn; Religious Conflict in Vietnam; Thich Tri Quang; Thích Trí Quang; buddhist activism; Ngô Đình Thục

01:24:41 - Ngô Đình Cẩn's Trial and Death

Play segment


Direct segment link:
interview36980.html#segment5081

Partial Transcript: Before May, the signs were already there?

Segment Synopsis: PXA discusses the trial and execution of Ngô Đình Cẩn following the 1963 coup. He states that Cẩn was tried by a military court under Nguyễn Khánh's government in 1964 for illegal actions against civilians. He describes how Cẩn smartly denied having any official power during the trial. PXA asserts that Cẩn was ultimately sentenced to death because he refused to give several million dollars from a Swiss bank account to General Khánh, choosing to give it to the Catholic Church instead. He states his belief that Cẩn would have been released if he had given the money to Khánh.

Keywords: 1964; Dương Văn Hiếu; Military Court; Nguyễn Khánh; Political trials; Trial; post-coup South Vietnam; Ngô Đình Cẩn

00:00:01EM: …Nayan Chanda, whom I think you knew very well.

00:00:05PXA: Yeah, I helped him when he first arrived here in the country. I briefed him about the military and the political situation.

00:00:14EM: Right. So, Edward rất hân hạnh có dịp gặp hôm nay.

00:00:20PXA: Thank you very much.

00:00:21EM: As I think you know, my advisor is Giáo Sư Hồ Huệ Tâm.

00:00:31PXA: Yeah, Hồ Huệ Tâm. This is the daughter of Hồ Hữu Tường. He was a professor of Mathematics at the secondary school in Cần Thơ.

00:00:39EM: Right, and a Trotskyite.

00:00:44PXA: A Trotskyite, and he was detained by the French, but after WWII, he was released—no, during WWII, he was released from jail because he is a Trotskyite, not Third International. Those who weren't Third International, they continued to detain. And he very bright, very bright, very good professor of mathematics. And his children are very bright, too. One of his daughters is a medical doctor.

00:01:18EM: Yes. Hồng Ðao.

00:01:20PXA: And another one is in London [inaudible]. All of them had the red insignia and like a red star [inaudible]. The name of this son had the kind of Communist symbol. [recall the name of Hồ Hữu Tường's son in Vietnamese] Hồ Xích Tú.

00:02:01Edward Miller: Cô ơi, chúng ta có thể đóng cửa?

00:02:12PXA: To close the door? Yeah, sure.

00:02:12Edward Miller: I'm worried that maybe we won't be able to hear or won't be able to record.

00:02:17PXA: [inaudible]

00:02:20Edward Miller: I think if we close the door, it'll be okay.

00:02:48PXA: [inaudible]

00:02:49EM: I think that's fine.

00:03:02PXA: [phrase to close the door; addressing his wife in Vietnamese about hot water]

00:03:12EM: In my research––my research is on Ngô Ðình Diệm and his relations with the United States. But in my research, I’ve also been spending some time looking at the internal politics of the Ngô Ðình Diệm government. Because I think that up until now, historians have not paid enough attention to these. I’m especially interested in the relationship among the Ngô brothers, because there were–it seems clear that there were many rivalries between the brothers. For example, between Ngô Ðình Nhu and Ngô Ðình Cẩn, and I’m wondering what you might be able to tell me about that.

00:04:06PXA: Actually, not rivalry, no.

00:04:10Edward Miller: Not a rivalry?

00:04:12PXA: Not a rivalry. On appearance, they were rivals, because Ngô Ðình Nhu was considered an intellectual. He got an education in France, while Ngô Ðình Cẩn, the youngest son and a very beautiful son, had to stay at home, take care of the mother—his mother—as well as the mother of the other. Ngô Ðình Thục, he lucky to become a bishop. And then Ngô Ðình Nhu, an intellectual. And Ngô Ðình Diệm, he was a mandarin, and then he became the President. But this man, actually, he worked very hard for the regime before the regime came to power–for the family.

00:05:00Edward Miller: Which one? Nhu or Cẩn?

00:05:03PXA: Cẩn.

00:05:03Edward Miller: Cẩn, what did he do specifically?

00:05:06PXA: He knows the people. He worked underground. He had a constituency in Huế, et cetera. So when the time came, Diệm became Prime Minister and then President later, and Nhu returned from France, et cetera. But all the men working for the regime were furnished by Ngô Ðình Cẩn. He's very smart.

00:05:34Edward Miller: Was that only in Central Vietnam or also in the South?

00:05:39PXA: Even here in the South, even the private secretary of Ngô Đình Nhu, actually the man of Cẩn.

00:05:45Edward Miller: Trần Kim Tuyến?

00:05:46PXA: No, Phạm Thư Đường.

00:05:49Edward Miller: Phạm Thư Đường was a man of Ngô Ðình Cẩn?

00:05:51PXA: Ngô Ðình Cẩn. He detected the man when he was recruited. He was drafted into the Vietnamese Reserve Officer Cadet School from North Vietnam, and graduated at the end, the first promotion. Assigned to Huế, he found out the guy was good, so he recruited the man. Like the colonel, and after that, he became General Đỗ Mậu.

00:06:22Edward Miller: Đỗ Mậu.

00:06:23PXA: Yeah, for security.

00:06:24Edward Miller: He was also recruited by Cẩn?

00:06:26PXA: By Cẩn.

00:06:27Edward Miller: And he was from Central Vietnam as well?

00:06:29PXA: Yeah, Central Vietnam, in Quảng Bình, I think. And many other Ngô Ðình Cẩn men.

00:06:36Edward Miller: I see, that’s very interesting. Now, at that time, before 1954, Ngô Ðình Cẩn was recruiting his people–

00:06:43PXA: He’s working underground. The French had followed him, secretly, but he was very smart. For instance, he bought–he helped the Buddhists. They called it the Bồ Đề school in Huế. Actually, he knows how to invest the money there.

00:07:05Edward Miller: Cẩn did?

00:07:05PXA: Cẩn did it! He owned that one. Secretly.

00:07:10Edward Miller: Secretly? Wow. That is very interesting, especially in light of the later relationships.

00:07:16PXA: But the reason is that he didn’t have enough education, no formal education. He just finished his primary school, that’s all. His behavior is like the old traditional Vietnamese way: son of a mandarin family, a mandarino family, well-known. His father and his grandfather were well-known in Huế. So he took care of his mother. So he is just the traditional Huế man, chewing betel all the time. He behaved like a dictator.

00:07:57Edward Miller: But his attitude, what you said about the Bồ Đề school is interesting to me, because it means he was perhaps different from Ngô Ðình Thục and Ngô Ðình Nhu in the way he cultivated, or patronized, support from the Buddhists.

00:08:12PXA: That’s right, he worked grassroots. While the other people, they don’t have their own institution–their own constituency. He’s a man who has.

00:08:25Edward Miller: That's very interesting. Now, at this time in the early 1950s, before 1954, when Diệm was in the United States and in Europe–

00:08:34PXA: He was in Japan, and then in China, and when China lost to Mao Zedong in 1949, the Cardinal—the Chinese Cardinal—advised the Americans to recruit the man. He knows Wesley Fishel, the young professor of Political Science at the University of Michigan–

00:09:03Edward Miller: Michigan State, yes.

00:09:05PXA: So that came through the recommendation of the Cardinal, before the Chinese Cardinal went to Taiwan or someplace, I forgot the name of that place.

00:09:16Edward Miller: I see. Let me ask you about Ngô Ðình Nhu. I’ve done a lot of research on Diệm and his activities in the U.S. during this time. But Nhu’s activities are harder to follow. I know he was involved in the publication of Xã Hội, the magazine in Saigon. So, while Cẩn is organizing at a grassroots level, that’s something that Nhu–

00:09:46PXA: All his men–men of action–are recruited by Cẩn.

00:09:50Edward Miller: What about Trần Quốc Bửu and the Vietnamese Confederation of Labor?

00:09:59PXA: He was a man–he was actually recruited by the French G2. He was with the Việt Minh first in 1945, et cetera, and he was trained by the Japanese.

00:10:13Edward Miller: Was he briefly working with the Cao Đài?

00:10:16PXA: That’s right, because at that training post in Cambodia, there was Cao Đài Trình Minh Thế and Trần Quốc Bửu, and the Communists–the Việt Minh General Nguyễn Bình.

00:10:35Edward Miller: Nguyễn Bình.

00:10:36PXA: Yeah, he's the same––graduated the same [training program]. And General Lâm Văn Phát. He died in California.

00:10:48Edward Miller: So they were all trained by the Japanese?

00:10:49PXA: By Japanese. The Japanese are very smart. They know how to infiltrate men, et cetera, and then recruit them. Like, they created the Hòa Hảo religion, they did it, and they know how to support the Cao Đàists and then control the Cao Đàists.

00:11:06Edward Miller: I see, so Trần Quốc Bửu and Trình Minh Thế have that relationship from the forties?

00:11:12PXA: That’s right, from the Japanese.

00:11:14Edward Miller: And then in the early fifties, Trần Quốc Bửu is cooperating with the Ngô brothers?

00:11:22Edward Miller: Trần Quốc Bửu? Yeah.

00:11:23PXA: Own brother? I don't know his own brother.

00:11:27Edward Miller: No, I mean the Ngô brothers.

00:11:28PXA: Oh, the Ngô brothers. Yeah, yeah. Later, later, because the French used him to lead the Catholic Working Federation–Worker Federation. They call it the–

00:11:49Edward Miller: Jeuneuse Ouvrière Catholique?

00:11:52PXA: No, no–yeah. They call it the–that’s Catholic? That’s right. Liên Ðoàn Lao Ðộng Thiên Chúa Giáo–Catholic Federation of Workers.

00:12:09Edward Miller: But that’s different from Bửu's Federation.

00:12:13PXA: That's different, because at that time the French invented this word. Bửu was made head of it because he was recruited by the French G2 to lead this one, against the Communist workers. Because they know the Communists––the French know the Communists recruit the workers and then the peasants—they call it the basic class. To counter them, they set up their own labor federation against the other federation of the Communists. So they used this man. But when Ngô Ðình Nhu came to power, he changed a little bit to make it sound less Catholic.

00:12:59Edward Miller: Trần Quốc Bửu himself was not Catholic?

00:13:06PXA: No, I don’t think he was Catholic, no. But the Americans know how to set up the new one from France in here, in order to compete with the French to control here in Vietnam. This was the Force Ouvrière.

00:13:25Edward Miller: Force Ouvrière?

00:13:26PXA: That is the creation of America in the U.S.—in France.

00:13:31Edward Miller: Really?

00:13:31PXA: Oh yeah! And that one had a representative here. The first representative is Mr. Trần Khánh Vân.

00:13:43Edward Miller: Trần Khánh Vân?

00:13:45PXA: Yeah, I don’t know whether he died or not, but he is a bit older then I. He should be born in 1923, ‘24. His office is near the Thanh Niên Restaurant.

00:14:01Edward Miller: Oh, really? Okay. So Bửu, by the early fifties, is working with the Ngô brothers but with the French as well, you're saying?

00:14:16PXA: Yeah, and when Ngô Ðình Diệm came to power, he was recruited by Diệm, too, particularly by Dr. Tuyến, et cetera. So he was made member of the Cần Lao party.

00:14:29Edward Miller: At that time?

00:14:31PXA: At that time.

00:14:33Edward Miller: But the relationship doesn’t last very long.

00:14:36PXA: No, he doesn’t last long.

00:14:40Edward Miller: And what was the source of the break, did it have to do with the strikes in 1956?

00:14:47PXA: 1956, 1955, 1956? Yeah, there was a strike '56. This was because after Diệm used the dictatorial policy, he controlled everything and he dissolved the village election, the traditional one. But, according to the Vietnamese, “Lệ vua thua lệ làng.”

00:15:25Edward Miller: The writ of the emperor stops at the village gate.

00:15:29PXA: So the Vietnamese were very upset about that, the villagers particularly. So he set up his own way. So in ‘56, when he was sure that he had the support of Americans to consolidate his family power. Even the opposition, the legal opposition—like Đại Việt, V.N.Q.D.D., the Hòa Hảo, the Cao Đài, et cetera—all of them were anti-Việt Minh, or anti-Communist for sure. Many of them cooperated with Việt Minh for a while at the beginning, because all of them were patriotic people. So, Diệm didn’t want them to be opposition in the government, so he considered them––outlawed all of them. Cao, Thiên, Hòa, Bình. All of them were outlawed. Cao means Cao Đài. Thiên, Thiên Chúa Giáo, Thiên Chúa Giáo in the South. And Hòa, Hòa Hảo. Bình, Bình Xuyên.

00:16:38Edward Miller: But what about Bửu and his unions? Where–

00:16:44PXA: So he continued to work. And Dr. Tuyến is smart––he divided––Dr. Tuyến is in charge of, the Chief of the Political and Social–Chính trị Xã hội–and Cultural Office. That includes also the secret police, too. He's not a professional intelligence officer now. But he's a man trusted by the Catholic Church to run the show, particularly in politics. And not intelligence, et cetera. He learned it later from the British and then from the American CIA.

00:17:29Edward Miller: So what was his––

00:17:32PXA: Tuyến [inaudible]. At the same time, Tuyến set up another labor organization.

00:17:38Edward Miller: I see. What was it called?

00:17:41PXA: Lực lượng Lao động.

00:17:42Edward Miller: Lực lượng Lao động?

00:17:45PXA: No no, not Lực lượng Lao động. By his own man. I asked him why he did it. He said very simple. If you have only one Federation, in case it gets infiltrated by the communists, they go on strike and we would be in a very bad position. So we should divide them. We have two of them to compete in order to counterbalance.

00:18:12Edward Miller: And when did he do that? Do you remember?

00:18:15PXA: Uh, he did that when he took over that office. That office was first run by, uh.

00:18:23Edward Miller: [inaudible]

00:18:25PXA: Sở Nghiên cứu Chính trị Xã Hội và Văn hoá––that office was first run by Mr. Vũ Tiến Huân.

00:18:35Edward Miller: I'm sorry. What's his name?

00:18:36PXA: Vũ Tiến Huân. H-U-A-N.

00:18:41PXA: Vũ Tiến Huân was a mandarin; he was Đốc phủ sứ. Only two North Vietnamese were made Đốc phủ sứ in the South. One is Trịnh Đình Thảo, who had a law degree. This one has administrative degree in Hanoi. That course was reserved for––even Ngô Đình Diệm––took that course in Hanoi. Administration school. But the South, because of colony, so the highest rank for them was the district Chief, not province Chief. But for Protectorate, they were made province Chief like Ngô Đình Diệm and the others. So that man––I had a mental block––I just mentioned––

00:19:34Edward Miller: Trịnh Đình Thảo? Or––

00:19:37PXA: Trịnh Đình Thảo and the other one is Vũ Tiến Huân. Vũ Tiến Huân, when the French returned, he was made Chief of Chợ Lớn province. At that time, Chợ Lớn became a province. Under the French, Chợ Lớn is a province.

00:19:52Edward Miller: In 1945 this was?

00:19:55PXA: Before '45, Chợ Lớn is a province, Gia Định not a province. Now both of them merged together to make Hồ Chí Minh City. Then Chợ Lớn has their own mayor, and Saigon their own mayor too. Then Vũ Tiến Huân was made by the French, when the French returned, the province Chief of Chợ Lớn.

00:20:20Edward Miller: Chợ Lớn.

00:20:21PXA: And Ngô Đình Thục's family, particularly Ngô Đình Diệm, when he returned from Europe or from the U.S. or from Japan, he went to his friend in Chợ Lớn. That's why he became a good friend of Vũ Tiến Huân. Vũ Tiến Huân protects these people. So that's why when he came to power, he made him head of that one, but he's not Catholic.

00:20:51Edward Miller: Huân was not Catholic?

00:20:52PXA: Huân was not Catholic. He's a good friend of my father. I know him very well. He liked the movie, he liked pictures, et cetera.

00:20:59PXA: He was in Gia Định before, and he was made chief of that one. But after that and the reorganization, they used their trusted man, so Tuyến was made head of that one in 19––late '56.

00:21:16 to Nhu>?

00:21:26PXA: No, he close to the church.

00:21:30Edward Miller: The church. So Thục? Was he recruited by Ngô Đình Thục?

00:21:35PXA: No, by the church.

00:21:36Edward Miller: By the church?

00:21:38PXA: Bùi Chu, Phát Diệm, or someplace.

00:21:40Edward Miller: Was he from the North?

00:21:41PXA: Yeah. He from Thanh Hoá.

00:21:43Edward Miller: Thanh Hoá? I see.

00:21:46PXA: He intended to be the Catholic priest. He attended the seminars. But then he learned, after that, he got the degree of Literature––Cử nhân Văn chương. After that, he took another course called the medical school.

00:22:13Edward Miller: In Hanoi?

00:22:14PXA: In Hanoi. And then where he met the midwife who became later his wife. He was in love with that midwife, so he quit being a seminarist and married this lady and became a doctor.

00:22:32PXA: But doctor without thesis. Do you know why? Because he was drafted into the army. So those who go to medical school, they are authorized to go there to attend the first five years. After the sixth year, you prepare your thesis, and then after graduation, at the seventh year, you got the Doctor degree.

00:22:57PXA: But the French were very smart. They drafted at the end of the fifth year and to serve the army as a medical doctor. But when they were dismissed or they were demobilized, they weren't allowed to write the thesis that they experienced during the war––to write the thesis and to get the doctorate degree. We had many doctors without thesis, so they cannot practice their profession, like Dr. Tuyến and Dr. Đàm Quang Trung, et cetera.

00:23:30Edward Miller: I see because they had been drafted into the army before they wrote the thesis and then afterwards they didn't––

00:23:35PXA: Afterwards, they were not––they could not open the cabinet, the medical cabinet. You are a doctor, but you don't know how to to give a shot to the people. I can do it better than you. He's a good friend of mine.

00:23:54Edward Miller: Yes. I read about that in, AJ Langguth's book.

00:24:04PXA: He helped me a lot when I applied for the visa. Very difficult to get at that time. I had a lot of problems.

00:24:14Edward Miller: You mean to go to the United States?

00:24:15PXA: Yeah. Even when the American agree everything, but on the Vietnamese side, they were very tough. But then when I returned, I applied to work for him, and he agreed because I had a friend working for Ngô Đình Cẩn. He's the chief of Police and Security of Central Vietnam.

00:24:38Edward Miller: Who was he?

00:24:39PXA: Mr. Lê Khắc Duyệt.

00:24:41Edward Miller: Lê Khắc Duyệt?

00:24:42PXA: Yeah, he's a relative of Lê Khắc Quyến. Many Lê Khắc's joined the revolution in the North. That's a very well-known family in Huế.

00:24:53Edward Miller: So you were in the United States at what time?

00:24:57PXA: '57 to '59. I went there October 10th and returned October 8th.

00:25:03Edward Miller: So you you came back in in 1959? And this Lê Khắc Duyệt helped you?

00:25:13PXA: I applied to work for him because I was not––because many of our people were already arrested. My boss too, Mr. Hương, et cetera. All of them in 1957 and '58. 85% of cadres left in South Vietnam were either arrested or killed, most of them killed.

00:25:37Edward Miller: 85%?

00:25:38PXA: 85% out of 60,000 left behind. Hardcores in Cochinchina. I don't know about Central Vietnam or High Plateau, but Cochinchina, that's important, because it includes Chợ Lớn, Gia Định et cetera–that's the headquarter.

00:25:56Edward Miller: So the policies were very effective?

00:25:59PXA: Very efficient, very efficient. Ngô Đình Cẩn did it.

00:26:05Edward Miller: So Ngô Đình Cẩn––

00:26:07PXA: Ngô Đình Cẩn did it, not Ngô Đình Nhu or Dr. Tuyến. No no no, Ngô Đình Cẩn did it.

00:26:12Edward Miller: Really? So even in South Vietnam, it was Ngô Đình Cẩn––

00:26:16PXA: Ngô Đình Cẩn who did that. He kidnapped them. He did not use the law, because to arrest the people, you should have the law, et cetera. The legacy of French administration: if you have a suspect, you can detain him; you call it preventive detention, but you cannot send him to jail. You see the point there? But for Ngô Đình Cẩn, forget about that. You just kidnapped and took them to Huế.

00:26:47Edward Miller: To Huế?

00:26:48PXA: To Huế, there'd be all kind of underground prison, et cetera. They have here in [Tân Hội?] a place to keep these people that they kidnap in the street, and another place here on Lê Văn Duyệt Street. The two places, they kidnapped them and they took to Huế, under the protection of Tuyến, because he was Chief of police and everything. He oversees; he was not director.

00:27:26Edward Miller: This is [Lê Khắc Duyệt?]

00:27:27PXA: [Lê Khắc Duyệt?]. He was also a very nice man. He was functionaire under the French, and then he was made Chief police under the French. And Ngô Đình Cẩn know him, know that he's very not naughty, and he's a good government cadre because he is from Huế, so he knows all the big families. So he used the man, he know that the man is very loyal to the regime––any regime. The French trained that way: if you are made functionaire, you'd just be loyal to the the system. You are not politician, so you have no problem. See it? So he know that. Good one. He's Buddhist probably too, but Ngô Đình Cẩn––he's Catholic, et cetera. He's surrounded by a lot of Catholics. These Catholics, you know, used tricks to push Ngô Đình Cẩn to get rid of this man.

00:28:32Edward Miller: Oh, really?

00:28:33PXA: Yeah. How are you to have the one Chief of police, he's a Buddhist? In the meantime, you are Catholic. Your parent, your father, et cetera, Catholic, et cetera. The regime is for the Catholic, but you have one Chief of Secret Police and Security and Police of Central Vietnam––a Buddhist. That is very dangerous.

00:28:59Edward Miller: When did that happen? When did Cẩn get rid of––?

00:29:02PXA: No, he didn't get rid of him. He did not get rid of this one. He yelled at the other one. He scolded them. He said, look, you people, you are a flatterer, troublemaker.

00:29:20Edward Miller: He's talking to his Catholic supporters?

00:29:23PXA: Yeah, the Catholic supporters. He scolded them. He said, look, I know this man. He's not naughty, he's very human. Even though if he see, you kill a chicken, if you cut the head of a chicken––the Vietnamese way of killing, not like American. He couldn't––he closed his eyes, and sometimes he fainted by looking at that. So he's very human. So I used him, and he loyal, he report everything to me that he knows. For instance, if I mad––I can get mad very easily, I have hot temper. If I heard something, I said alright, kill him. And if I tell it to you, you automatically kick him out and kill him. But Duyệt, when I tell him alright, this VC is very bad, kill him––but he dared not do it. He knows my temperament, he just keep it. He did not report that he kill or not, et cetera. One week later, I change my mind. I feel repent not by doing that, because that's too much, because that's suspected, not real, concrete. I said alright, have you killed that man yet? He said, not yet, because I know that you have hot temper. But if now you decide, I will kill. No, no, now I change my mind. Alright, let him leave. You see? If the other one is Catholic, automatically they are flatterer. He is so smart that way. But here, they look down upon him in Saigon. Saigon is intellectual, et cetera, than Central Vietnamese. But this is the Lý trưởng. Lý trưởng that means a village official––they call it Lý trưởng in Central Vietnam. And the youngest son of the family, Út trầu––they gave him all kind of titles. And he was stupid––

00:31:27Edward Miller: To?

00:31:28PXA: To Ngô Đình Cẩn. The people in Central Vietnam, in South Vietnam, particularly intellectuals from Hanoi and intellectuals from Saigon, they considered Ngô Đình Cẩn a stupid man, fool around, you know?

00:31:45Edward Miller: But in fact, they didn't appreciate how effective he was?

00:31:48PXA: They did not know, and they looked down upon him. And when the coup happened in 1960––you know, the November coup. Actually the coup was orchestrated by Durbrow, Elbridge Durbrow, the ambassador.

00:32:07Edward Miller: Durbrow?

00:32:07PXA: He was official of the American embassy in Moscow. He was assigned here first when Diệm became president, et cetera. He replaced Reinhardt––Frederick Reinhardt, the ambassador. Frederick Reinhardt came here to replace the special envoy, General Lawton Collins. So when they pulled a coup, the coup failed, just to intimidate Diệm, to force him to reorganize his administration. Put pressure on him, that's all, but not to get rid of him yet. That's the first sign that Americans need to be involved here more, et cetera. That's a very long story. Yeah. So the coup was over. But before the coup happened, Ngô Ðình Cẩn, he sent here a telegram, a long report that a coup is going to happen against the regime in a very short time.

00:33:27Edward Miller: This was before the coup took place?

00:33:29PXA: Before the coup took place––Excuse me [coughing]. So and then I asked Dr. Tuyến, et cetera.

00:33:39Edward Miller: I'm sorry. You asked who?

00:33:41PXA: He sent a report to Ngô Ðình Nhu, to inform him in advance that the coup is going to happen. But Ngô Ðình Nhu looked down upon his young brother–– not only his young brother, but he was not intellectual. He didn't know much. You know. And he sent over. And how could he know the situation in Saigon? You see? So. And he checked in the waste bucket. But the other one. Pick it up. They are not to burn it.

00:34:14Edward Miller: Who picked it up?

00:34:16PXA: The man of of Ngo Dinh Nhu [inaudible] the pick up in order not to burn it. But nobody knew. He was so mad.

00:34:22Edward Miller: Just. Right. Right.

00:34:23PXA: Squeeze it and throw it in the waste basket.

00:34:26Edward Miller: Right.

00:34:27PXA: But it was safe.

00:34:27Edward Miller: And did twin twin tell you this?

00:34:30PXA: Some people– no. He didn't know about that. Yeah. And the other people would know about it. They told me about that.

00:34:36Edward Miller: I see.

00:34:36PXA: So I checked with [inaudible]. All right. That's true. But I would like to go there to talk to Ngo Dinh Can about that. So I asked my cousin. I mean, the chief of security there to introduce me and then that I would like to interview him, to write a story or write it. At that time, I worked for Reuters. Write about the coup d'état. And he is the man who was supposed to save the regime. It's very important. And you know about that. And I said, sure, but let me ask it first. So Ngo Dinh Can agreed to see me, you know, at least someone knows about that. Besides, he and his security and knew.

00:35:21Edward Miller: Right.

00:35:21PXA: Anyway, so he agreed to meet me. So very early in the morning, I was driven to his, you know, the fishing house. You know.

00:35:32Edward Miller: In Huế?

00:35:33PXA: In Huế, Cửa Thuận beach. Very beautiful house. Beautiful or not. We got up very early in the morning and ready to fish, et cetera.

00:35:44Edward Miller: I see.

00:35:45PXA: He enjoy life that way.

00:35:48Edward Miller: So this was right after the coup?

00:35:51PXA: After the coup about–

00:35:52Edward Miller: 1960?

00:35:54PXA: After 1960.

00:35:56Edward Miller: So 1961?

00:35:57PXA: '61 or something like that, yeah. November '60 I went there, I think January or December '60 or '61. I don't remember. But I wish to have a good story. And ask him about that, et cetera. He said yes, I did it, et cetera. So I want to know. The reason is because Mr. Nhu said that you don't know anything. Frankly speaking. You know, I'm suddenly–I'm very frank. I repeat what I heard And then Dr. Tuyến and many other people said that you don't know much. You just, you know, know only in Huế that's so. Yeah. But not much. And but what–my curiosity is, please tell me, how do you know about that? That's what I wish to know. He said: "Very simple. I arrested almost all the Communist agents in Saigon, including those sent from North Vietnam. See that? So I kidnapped them and took them to Huế. So my brother didn't know the security. He didn't know. I just kidnapped them. That's all very simple."

00:37:15Edward Miller: Right, but the coup was carried out by VNQDD, right?

00:37:20PXA: Yeah. By the other. So these are VCs. They have the duty to follow everything. Military? Not much. No military because fighting, but political activity. And they follow all the political parties in the South and religion. That's their assignment to follow them. Because for political struggling after the signing of the Geneva Agreement, '54 to '56 for election. And now, no election, et cetera.

00:37:59PXA: See that? So they carry all kind of activity against the regime.

00:38:04Edward Miller: Right.

00:38:05PXA: So I realized with the American visa supported by the American and SEATO, et cetera, it takes very long, long time for the communists to take over. But our regime here, my brother regime, can be overthrown by these damn nationalists.

00:38:29Edward Miller: I see.

00:38:31PXA: Nationalist opposition. So to know them. Very simple. Like calling capture VC and North Vietnamese telling them to report– those who agree– to report their knowledge about the activity of the opposition, those who put the code, those who attempt code, et cetera. tell me I keep it secret. I wouldn't reveal your name or anything. I keep my promise. But after that, I released you and you agree. And then you continue your activity by following these people and then report to me secretly through our man, you know, without anyone knowing about that. So the communists don't know that you were captured either. You are there. So I–you told me. Can you ask a Catholic to step on the cross? No. No. Catholic. They had to step on the cross of Jesus Christ.

00:39:43Edward Miller: Right.

00:39:44PXA: So you ask the communists to fight against communists. Let's see. No sense, no use. They would lie or they would never tell you the truth.

00:39:56Edward Miller: Right.

00:39:56PXA: So you have the way to let them have the chance [you're not to work for us is to denounce] those who–the most immediate threat to the regime. So they report what they know about that, and what they heard about that. Then I ordered my men to follow these people to Saigon, here and etcetera, in the countryside. That's why I know that the coup is going to happen in the military people, thanks to the VC that I capture.

00:40:32Edward Miller: Because he was following them. He knew that the VC that were captured would not––

00:40:36PXA: Their profession is to follow these people, and to push them to carry activity against the regime.

00:40:42Edward Miller: So the VC then had penetrated the VNQDD and the other groups

00:40:47PXA: Everyone, everywhere. So Ngô Đình Cẩn is very smart. I said, all right, thank you very much. I will write a story about that, but not to go too detailed. "All right, but before you write, you let me know. You publish, you let me know." So I returned to Saigon. I talked to Ngô Đình Nhu's people. "You thought Ngô Đình Cẩn is stupid. He's not stupid. He's smarter than you people!" He remembered by heart all the names, even the commander of the second Military Corps. General at that time–Colonel Tôn Thất Đính.Ngô Đình Nhu's people. "You thought Ngô Đình Cẩn is stupid. He's not stupid. He's smarter than you people!" He remembered by heart all the names, even the commander of the second Military Corps. General–at that time, Colonel–Tôn Thất Đính.

00:41:26PXA: He said that is stupid. You know the Indigène Garde [Garde Indigène]. You know, khố xanh khố đỏ [blue and red belt]. [inaudible] He recruited his people, he made them general, he made them colonel, et cetera.

00:41:41Edward Miller: So Cẩn recruited Tôn Thất Đính?

00:41:42PXA: Yeah, Tôn Thất Đính too! You look at it, he's so stupid! He confiscated the FULRO, you know, carry the activity, and some FULRO followed the VC. He ordered to confiscate everything, including the arrow and bow. How can they make a living? They should use it to kill the animal. You confiscate their weapon.

00:42:16Edward Miller: Who ordered this? This was Cẩn?

00:42:18PXA: Ngô Đình–Tôn Thất Đính!

00:42:21Edward Miller: Tôn Thất Đính, when he was in the Highlands?

00:42:23PXA: Yea, so Ngô Đình Cẩn called him in and said you are stupid! You should return it to them, but you confiscate all the weapon. But that's why you had to return to it.

00:42:36Edward Miller: So Ngô Đình Cẩn, it seems, at least for a while, his strategies were very effective?

00:42:41PXA: Very effective.

00:42:42Edward Miller: And he was–he seems to have been less Catholic than his brothers, in the sense that he did not rely only on Catholics. He tried to win support of other groups.

00:42:55PXA: He tried to build constituency, because he carried secret activity under the French. His family actually worked together with Ngô Đình Thục.

00:43:09Edward Miller: With Ngô Đình Thục.

00:43:10PXA: Ngô Đình Thục was the leader of the family. And Ngô Đình Thục is a friend of [Francis] Cardinal Spellman. Both of them were promoted bishop at the same time by Vatican. The other one was Bishop of New York, while this one was Bishop of Vĩnh Long. The first bishop in Vietnam, and they were good friends. And you know, the P XII [Pope Pius XII], he worked for the American intelligence.

00:43:36Edward Miller: I'm sorry. Who?

00:43:38PXA: The Pope.

00:43:40Edward Miller: The Pope?

00:43:41PXA: He worked for the U.S. intelligence. And then he knows how to put these two guys together. That's why, under the directive of Cardinal Spellman, Ngô Đình Thục know how to get in touch with the Catholics, who saw the Việt Minh in the jungle, including Phạm Ngọc Thảo, the son of his friend, Adrian Phạm Ngọc Thuần. The father of Phạm Ngọc Thảo. So he told Adrian to tell Thảo if something interesting, just give me the report. So he did it.

00:44:19Thục?

00:44:20PXA: This is Thục in Vĩnh Long.

00:44:24Edward Miller: And when did this happen?

00:44:26PXA: During the fight against the French. Thảo was in the jungle. He worked for the intelligence over there.

00:44:31Edward Miller: Okay, but that was the time that Thục started relationship with Thảo?

00:44:37PXA: That's right.

00:44:39PXA: Yeah, that's why–and many other stories. What I mean is Ngô Đình Thục and Cardinal Spellman knew each other a long time ago, and both of them work for the American authorities secretly against the French. You see the point there? Particularly when in 1950, when the French lost too much money, et cetera, and their budget is too small. The Expeditionary Corps need a lot of supplies and someone to foot the bill; if not, they have to end the war. But the Americans have to continue the war because they have a planetary policy against the Cold War. That's why the American president agreed to foot the bill for the French Expeditionary Corps. That's why they signed the agreement in 1950. And then with two conditions. This is–they call these two conditions come from the Wilson Doctrine.

00:45:51Edward Miller: I'm sorry. The Wilson Doctrine?

00:45:55PXA: Self determination for all the colonies. So that's the World War One, right after Woodrow Wilson's Doctrine, they call it self determination. So the American ask the French government, you have two things to do: Set up a Vietnamese government and set up the Vietnamese armed forces. And the French agreed, and then they sent a marshal–de Lattre de Tassigny–to do it.

00:46:29Edward Miller: Yeah. That's that's clear from the American documents that they're pushing the French in that regard. But if we could go back to Ngô Đình Cẩn for a second and his relationship with with Ngô Đình Thục. So did you end up publishing that story?

00:46:47PXA: No, in the end, it wasn't very good. But please, the people mouth, very dangerous. We Vietnamese have a saying "The tongue has no bone, the mouth has no ring." So you can say different ways.

00:47:12Edward Miller: So you thought it was too dangerous for you?

00:47:14PXA: No, for him.

00:47:16Cẩn said–

00:47:18PXA: Cẩn said "Alright, good story, but please don't publish it for my sake." So I will give you another favor if you want to. I know you love animal, so I will give you any animal you like. But he likes me very much.

00:47:35Edward Miller: I see. Okay. What about after 1960? In around the same time as the coup, Ngô Đình Thục became Archbishop of Huế.

00:47:51PXA: He wanted to be Archbishop here. But he got objection of the people, and particularly Vatican, so he dared not go too far. That's why they have here well known Paul Nguyễn Văn Bình.

00:48:08Edward Miller: Right? Right. And so Thục does not become Archbishop of Saigon, but becomes Archbishop of Huế. Does that mean that that Cẩn's influence is reduced?

00:48:21PXA: No, not reduced. He worked grassroots. And then his problem was this: he shared with me [inaudible] entente. That means the understanding between Ngô Đình Cẩn and Nhu and Diệm, because they know under their authority there's all kind of people: ministers, officials, officers, et cetera. Those were met Cẩn in Central Vietnam, they come and report to Nhu.

00:49:03Edward Miller: To Nhu?

00:49:04PXA: And those who met Nhu, they went to Huế to report to Cẩn. Right. So they make believe they were rivalry, in order to get the report of the disillusioned people working under them, in order to control them, to follow them in the future. So it's smart. They are so smart.

00:49:22Edward Miller: Nhu and Cẩn really didn't have a rivalry. They were just pretending?

00:49:27PXA: Like one throw the ball, the other one catch the ball.

00:49:32Edward Miller: Okay. And how did–

00:49:39PXA: But sometime he met––he loved animals, but because of because of the flatterer. The important thing is the sycophant is very dangerous.

00:49:51Edward Miller: The Catholics in Central Vietnam?

00:49:53PXA: Catholic or anyone. That's why you read The Prince of Machiavelli. He taught the prince how to avoid flatterer. So anyone you need advice, just ask. But if not anyone come to give you an idea; that one is a flatterer. That's why Ngô Đình Cẩn is very smart. He's much smarter than Nhu. He's much smarter than Thục.

00:50:19Edward Miller: Well if Cẩn had been so effective against the Đảng Cộng Sản up until the late 1950’s–

00:50:33PXA: You know, eighty-five percent out of sixty thousand killed or captured by the Diệm regime are mainly by Ngô Ðình Cẩn people.

00:50:46Edward Miller: Mainly by Ngô Ðình Cẩn. And if that was the case, why did it change after the 1950’s? Because obviously the party makes a comeback and becomes much stronger. Why were Cẩn’s techniques no longer effective?

00:51:02PXA: Cẩn’s technique? He created animosity, he created hatred. Many of them joined the Việt Minh because they loved their country–they’re patriots, including the Cao Đài, Hòa Hảo, et cetera. They joined the Việt Minh, even the Đại Việt, too. Đại Việt, actually, was created by the Japanese. It was Komatsu who created the Đại Việt. Komatsu, he was Deputy Chief of Counter Role institute in Japan. He also control Trần Văn Chương–

00:51:43Edward Miller: Oh, really?

00:51:45PXA: Yeah. The father of–

00:51:47Trần Lệ Xuân.

00:51:48PXA: Trần Lệ Xuân and Trần Văn Thông, the family under control of Komatsu. And when the Americans return, they used him, so he gave reports all of Đại Việt to the Americans. And Americans recruit them, and accept. When the French return, 1945, they know how to use the Đại Việt, too. That’s why the Đại Việt is divided...those who work for the French, or those who work for the Americans, et cetera.

00:52:15Edward Miller: But my question is, why is it if Ngô Ðình Cẩn is so effective against the party, and the party is really weakened–

00:52:28PXA: Oh, they very weakened, especially in Central Vietnam, very, very tough.

00:52:32Edward Miller: Why does the situation change? Because it changes it seems to me very quickly—1959, 1960, '61—the party comes back and becomes much stronger.

00:52:41PXA: Yeah, that’s right. Actually, because of the people. Ngô Ðình Diệm's regime has no constituency. In Vietnam, you should use at least one constituency, either the army…in the past, under the French, or the French Army, the Vietnamese were suppletif [auxillary] force, you know, not a real army. But under Diệm, it’s different. With the American money, they build things very fast. But the main thing is the people. You have a mandarin from Huế who control everything. And then the family control everything, and they do not allow even loyal opposition, like those who fought against the Việt Minh. They were kicked out and outlawed, too. Many of them were captured and killed, too. So all of them gang together, that’s a one. The peasant, the peasant rely on what? On the land. And the land was confiscated. Because they were dispossessed, they were sent into first, the Agroville in 1960. When I reported first to Dr. Tuyến, the Agroville were not appreciated, so he start over, to set up the Strategic Hamlet Program, the same thing but smaller size. And so they were disposed of, dispossessed of their land and their ancestral village. They had to go into the Agroville to live and to go outside five, ten kilometers by sampan to grow rice, et cetera. They just separate them from the Communist cadres. But when they go there, the Communists are still there, you see it, because they listen to the Chinese, because the Communist slogan is this: "The cadre and the people are like the water and the fish." So, if you just take out the water, the fish die. But you take out the water, the fish follow the water and go inside. So, that's why. The second important thing: in Vietnam, they had a village election that the French respected and Ngô Ðình Diệm get rid of it in 1956. And another law, any Chinese or foreigner living in Vietnam, born in Vietnam, should take Vietnamese–

00:55:43Edward Miller: Nationality.

00:55:44PXA: Citizenship. Those who don’t want to do it, just out of the government and no business, et cetera. It’s difficult. Only one who dare to oppose, he so proud of himself, and you know his name, Nguyễn Văn Điềm, engineer. Mr. Nguyễn Văn Điềm, engineer. He speak French, he prefer to speak French better than Vietnamese; he speak English very well, too. And then he’s Director-General of Planning for Diệm, when Diệm became president, et cetera, for very long time. Those work for him are very well-known too, including Vũ Văn Thái. The one who works with–

00:56:33<c.458: Edward Miller> He's director of the Office of Foreign Aid.

00:56:35PXA: Yeah, and then he work with the one who get the Pentagon paper and leak out–

00:56:42Edward Miller: Ellsberg.

00:56:43PXA: Ellsberg! Afterwards he work for the U.N. or something like that, Vũ Văn Thái. So, that man, the rest of them, have to take Vietnamese citizenship in order to continue business. So he create more and more animosity, more enemy intellectual. He could not get the intelligent to support him. All the intellectuals who would like to have, you call it, profiter, opportunist. He had to have position in the army, in the government, in business, et cetera, but in very small circles. So those on the outside hate these people, you see it? So the only way to them is to give support to the V.C. or the Việt Minh, particularly the Việt Minh. They don’t know much about Communism because the Communists very smart: they never talk Communism. Even now, for instance, they talk about Communism, but they don’t follow it. When they took over the government according to the teaching of Marx, you know what happen? The government fades out.

00:58:01Edward Miller: Right, the government would whither away.

00:58:04PXA: Whither away! We translate in Vietnamese “Tiêu vong,” that mean “die”—more serious. But ask the Communist party, they die only when they are overthrown by the people or when they have implosion like the Soviet Union. So if you ask the cadre, particularly the politician, when you take over the government, "How about that one? Why you continue all the time, when you whither out?" And then they refuse to answer.

00:58:37Edward Miller: I see. So let me ask you about–

00:58:45PXA: So Ngô Ðình Cẩn, I went there. See, I give you some anecdote, many anecdote. He like a cow, with a cow milk. So, the people in Saigon, particular people in Huế, know that he like cow milk, fresh milk. But they have Bến Cát here, you know Bến Cát Dairy farm?

00:59:09Edward Miller: Oh Bến Cát.

00:59:11PXA: Run by Mr. Carter, he was Colonel, he was Colonel during World War II. He was Colonel of the Australian Air Force, but he join the R.A.F., Royal Air Force. He married an Egyptian, a wing commander. So he was hero, but in Vietnam nobody know about that. So he was hired by Mr. Highland to run the dairy farm and Bến Cát here, actually to recruit–

00:59:45Edward Miller: What was his name?

00:59:46PXA: I forget his name, it was Carter something–

00:59:49Edward Miller: Carter.

00:59:50PXA: But it easy, you can find it in any book about the dairy farm in Bến Cát, run by Mr. Highland.

00:59:57Edward Miller: Highland.

00:59:59PXA: Highland, Australian businessman here. He run the business of the feather, of the duck feather, of the dairy farm. And he captured by the Communists, and then it was Bob Chaplain who negotiated with the Australian Burchett to release—

01:00:20Edward Miller: Burchett, oh, Wilfred Burchett.

01:00:22PXA: You know Burchett. Yes, he’s a Communist, pro-Communist. He would like to have the visa to go to U.S. but the U.S. refuse to give it to him, to see someone et cetera. And Bob Shaplen you know, Bob Shaplen, he’s a good friend of mine, he is working for the New Yorker. So he said, "Alright, I’ll make arrangements. You can order the Vietnamese to release Mr. Highland”—he was captured during the Tet Offensive—“and then I will tell American Embassy to give you the visa to the U.S.” So the deal was made, so that’s why he was released anyway. So when the Communists, they need something, they capture the guy. Kidnap Bến Cát, they kidnap the guy, in Bến Cát. It was in November, I think. November '61.

01:01:14November '61.

01:01:15PXA: He was kidnapped. There were Vietnamese working for him. After that, Vietnamese worked for Mr. Douglas and then for Neil Sheehan at UPI.

01:01:27Edward Miller: What was his name?

01:01:28PXA: Rao, Nguyễn Ngọc Rao. He was translator.

01:01:32Edward Miller: Nguyễn Ngọc Rao?

01:01:33PXA: Nguyễn Ngọc Rao, R-A-O. The North Vietnamese, they don’t know how to pronounce their R’s well, so actually, he should be written in Vietnamese, “Nguyễn Ngọc Giáo.” But the North Vietnamese...Rao Reo Rao, you know, so they put “Rao.” And that colonel was never revealed until he was captured. And then he was captured, and then I was busy to cover the flood, the Mekong Delta Châu Đốc, because most current-run advisors [mumbles] invited to go to have a look at the flood. And then, so we stay at the province chief, Colonel Minh, lieutenant colonel...at that time he was major chief of province. Nguyễn Văn Minh. After that, he became two star general, major general, commander of Saigon command and then the Third Corps, too. And then, all of Michigan State University went there, and then Walt Rostow and then Maxwell B. Taylor went there, too. This is combat troops.

01:02:48Edward Miller: November 1961. Okay.

01:02:50PXA: November ‘61. So over there we listen, we had a cable, telling us to follow very closely the writer, the capture of the guy in Bến Cát, the Egyptian, and they gave the biography he was full Colonel Air Force. They keep it secret so the Communists did not know that. They capture him because they need stationary, typewriter, and all kinds of thing, et cetera. So they ask him to tell his people to buy that in Hong Kong for them. So after, they supply this kind of thing, he was released.

01:03:28Edward Miller: He was released for stationary?

01:03:30PXA: For stationary, including the typewriter and the paper. He kidnapped by the guerilla in Bến Cát. But the purpose of that one is very important. He was near D-zone. You know, there two important zone in the South, they call it D-zone and then the other one is, close one is Tây Ninh, another military zone. So they set up this one here, so you recruit the worker to get intelligence, work at the dairy farm. You see the point there? Another zone. Military zone. So they set up this one here. So you recruit the worker to get intelligence, you know, work on the dairy farm. You see the point there, you set up a dairy farm in Bến Cát? Yeah, near the communist military zone. So recruit local people to get that. At the same time, you train them to select the one, the good one, to train them in intelligence. To get information for the government and then for the American and Australian here. You see the point? But they didn't know about that. They kidnapped him just for stationery.

01:04:37Edward Miller: I see, so the Americans were using the dairy farm to get intelligence?

01:04:41PXA: The Australians.

01:04:42Edward Miller: The Australians were using––

01:04:44PXA: Working for the Americans.

01:04:45Edward Miller: I see, were using the dairy farm to get intelligence.

01:04:47PXA: Yeah, so Ngô Ðình Cẩn, he heard that in Saigon they have fresh milk. The Ngô Ðình Cẩn people, to flatter him, they ask the people in Saigon to get him one or two cows, good ones, to send to Hue—when Ngô Ðình Cẩn, he like dog, he like birds, he like everything. He like animal, like Ngô Ðình Diệm too, he like nature...and so then he like the German shepherd. And then Phạm Quốc Thuần, the Minister of Defense. After that he was deputy, he was minister at the palace, Nguyễn Quốc Thuần—Phạm Quốc Thuần.

01:05:32Edward Miller: Phạm Quốc Thuần.

01:05:34PXA: Yeah, and then order this man to get two German shepherds. So they have plenty of German shepherds bought by the Americans given to the Vietnamese army and trained at Bến Cát...trained at not very far from here, they call the place they train German shepherds for operation. They select good ones to send to Ngô Ðình Cẩn, and Ngô Ðình Cẩn very happy. You know, the flatterer very dangerous, very dangerous are the flatterer; they wait until Mr. Thuần, you know, Phạm Quốc Thuần, returned to Saigon and they report to Cẩn.

01:06:20Edward Miller: And they brought the cows up to Huế?

01:06:24PXA: These people brought the cows already. This time, two German shepherds. And good ones, you what I mean? Well-trained and very– you can use it to attack or order him to do anything [phone rings]…This time two German shepherds, Phạm Quốc Thuần, you know. The minister brought two, because he minister, I think, of defense, and brought two dogs from the German shepherd training…So over there, and they didn’t say anything. He look at the dog and they very, very nice. And the flatterer does work for him say, “Alright take care of the dog,” so he took the dog, I’m going to talk to him for a while and Mr. Thuần returns to Saigon. They wait until Mr. Thuần returns to Saigon. They come and talk to Ngô Ðình Cẩn. They say, “Ông cậu”—they call him “Ông”—“Minister look down upon you, he has no regard for you, he gave you the dog but he doesn't give the name. How can you call the dog in? While you’re chewing betel, how you call him? [makes clicking sound, calling a dog] You can call him that way? While chewing it, you have to spit out the betel and call in the dog. [clicking sound] And you call him that way he couldn't come. You see it? He is so hot, arrogant. He look at you, representative of Central Vietnam—nothing!” You see that, you see the sign of the Minister, he very mad about that. He told me that, you know?

01:08:19Edward Miller: The minister you’re talking about, you said, is this Nguyễn Quốc Thuần?

01:08:23PXA: No, Phạm Quốc Thuần, I think...or Nguyễn Quốc Thuần, something like that. You check the...

01:08:29Edward Miller: He was Minister of the Economy?

01:08:31PXA: No, Minister of Defense. He had replaced

01:08:34Edward Miller: Trần Trung Dung.

01:08:40PXA: He had replaced Trần Trung Dung, Nguyễn Quốc Thuần, I think, something like that, Nguyễn Quốc Thuần. After that he became minister of the presidency.

01:08:48Edward Miller: That’s right, and he spoke English very well, right? He was very close to many Americans.

01:08:54PXA: That’s right, that’s right. So he order his men to bring two dogs when he pay the visit to Ngô Ðình Cẩn.

01:09:03Edward Miller: Right, but the flatterers, the Catholics undermine him.

01:09:08PXA: He make the mistake of not telling, giving the name of the two dogs, and how to call him. They use it against Thuần because they don’t like Thuần. They know that Thuần is very close to Trần Trung Dung and Ngô Ðình Cẩn —uh, Ngô Ðình Nhu...not close to...So he select his own men, like the chief of Vietnamese press, Nguyễn Thái is his man.

01:09:34Edward Miller: Is whose man?

01:09:34PXA: Nguyễn Thái.

01:09:35Edward Miller: Yes, I know [of] Nguyễn Thái.

01:09:37PXA: He very nice, he's the man––

01:09:40EM: And he was a man of Thuần’s?

01:09:44PXA: Yeah, of Cẩn.

01:09:46EM: Of Cẩn, he was a man of Cẩn’s, really?

01:09:48PXA: From Huế.

01:09:49EM: He was from Huế as well?

01:09:51PXA: He was recruited by Cẩn people when the Americans decided to recruit the Vietnamese when they signed agreement with the French. They started recruiting Vietnamese who graduated from high school, the baccalaureate, to send to U.S. for training for five-, four-year university. About ten of them.

01:10:13EM: And Nguyễn Thái was one of them?

01:10:14PXA: Yes, but from Central Vietnam should be decided by Ngô Ðình Cẩn, you see that? He very smart. So he returned here, one of the first ten Vietnamese loyal to Diệm to return from the U.S. here, to serve the regime. And Nguyễn Thái one of them. You see his picture, very young, even though at that time, he about thirty-four, thirty-five years old.

01:10:46EM: So that’s Nguyễn Thái, and––

01:10:50PXA: I don’t know this one, this is the Filipino colonel, full Colonel Benson.

01:11:00EM: Valeriano?

01:11:01PXA: No, friend of Valeriano, Colonel Benson.

01:11:05EM: Benson?

01:11:06PXA: Yeah. This is Lieutenant Sharp of the Navy. They graduated from the Fort Bragg, psychological warfare. They came to Vietnam to work together.

01:11:20EM: That's Nguyễn Thái.

01:11:22PXA: I forgot the guy. This guy.

01:11:24EM: Okay. I'm sure––I think we should probably finish up here because I know you've not been feeling well. Let me ask you one more question, though, about the Buddhist movement in 1963, Phong trào Phật giáo. And of course, that begins in Huế. My question is, why does it begin in Huế? And is it a movement that's a reaction against Ngô Đình Cẩn or against Ngô Đình Thục?

01:11:55PXA: It's against Ngô Đình Thục, because Ngô Đình Thục would like to convert the people into Catholic in order to have the big number to be made cardinal. You cannot be made cardinal with a small number of Catholic power.

01:12:08EM: Right. So he needs he needs a lot of conversions.

01:12:11PXA: That's right, that's right. That's the reason. And Ngô Đình Cẩn forced them. That's why in Vietnam we have three kinds of Catholic: lay down Catholic, born Catholic. And the knee down Catholic, I mean flatterer who followed the regime by converting themselves into Catholic. The standing up Catholic laymen, those who married Catholic to become Catholic. There are three kinds of Catholics in Vietnam: Born Catholic, knee down Catholic, and then standing up Catholic.

01:12:47EM: Standing up––for if you marry? So do you think that at that time, if Ngô Đình Thục had not been made Archbishop of Huế, there would be no Buddhist movement because the relations between–

01:13:03PXA: The Buddhist movement is this, it belongs to the international Buddhist movement. They called it in the early 30s or something like that. The Buddhists know that if they don't get together, they can never be strong, like the Muslim or the Catholic. That's why they get together in Ceylon, to set up the unification of Buddhists, all the sects. That's what they call it Viet... The same for the Vietnamese, they call it Phật giáo Việt Nam Thống Nhất because of that one. The first unified one. And in Ceylon and Vietnam, they send there Mr.–he's now running the the Buddhist school here––high school––and confiscated by the government. He went there. He was born 1919, '18 or '19? So he went to that conference in over 30. And then the second one we had, in Japan. Third one was in Phnom Penh or something like that. So the Americans know the Buddhist, the majority of Vietnamese follow the Buddhist . They are not Buddhists, but they more or less follow, influenced by the Buddhist. And then––that's not Ngô Đình Diệm––he influenced it. [inaudible] So they have to build constituents by forcing that. It won't work. So the Americans know about that. So they have to work with the Buddhists in case things happen. And they will be ready. And they use Trí Quang. Trí Quang is very important. He's from Quảng Bình. He's from Võ Nguyên Giáp village. Đỗ Mậu was also from this village. So they all three came from the same village. Trí Quang, Đỗ Mậu, and Võ Nguyên Giáp, and many others. When the Việt Minh came to power, the family of Trí Quang give support to them. But because of the extremists. They call it three no's, if you follow the communist regime, you have three no's: No family, no religion, no country. You have three no's. You work for the world and the International. So three no's. That's why they burn one of the monks, such as the uncle of Trí Quang alive. For some reason, because that one had some land, et cetera. And the local people, the peasant class, followers of communists, et cetera, and it's stupid. Not highly political, highly educated. They killed the man by burning. That image impressed into the head of Trí Quang. That's why Thích Quảng Đức burn. Because of that.

01:16:47EM: Thích Quảng Đức burns?

01:16:49PXA: Because of that image, he urged Thích Quảng Đức to burn.

01:16:54EM: Trí Quang urged Thích Quảng Đức to burn himself?

01:16:56PXA: Yeah. That's his idea. And after that, many other monks burned themselves because of that image. And then he started working for French G2 against the Việt Minh. The French had all the documents brought into Saigon after the Geneva Agreement was signed, and Trí Quang went to Huế to carry his activity at the Từ Đàm pagoda. And Ngô Đình Cẩn people know about that. My cousin knows about that. So with the American advisors, they have to treat them very well. In the future, they know that if you make them mad, they will against the regime––they will be against the regime. So the Americans used the Buddhists as a reserve card. I see.

01:17:46EM: But at first, the relationship between Ngô Đình Cẩn and the Buddhists was good?

01:17:50PXA: Always good, always good.

01:17:54EM: But why did it go bad?

01:17:56PXA: Go bad because––

01:17:58EM: Because of Thục?

01:17:59PXA: Because of Thục. When the other people––because Thục did not want––You know, in Huế family, traditional family, the young people should take the order of the elders. Not only that, but he's also the bishop––archbishop, not bishop.

01:18:16EM: He has a lot of authority.

01:18:18PXA: Yes, authority. So Ngô Đình Cẩn agreed to follow to forbid the flags. And the people were very mad about that, so they demonstrated. And then Ngô Đình Thục ordered his men to throw the grenade.

01:18:40EM: To throw the grenade?

01:18:41PXA: Yeah. Many killed. That's very bad.

01:18:45EM: Because I read the the Hồi ký of Trí Quang in 1964 or '65. He published in Tạp chí Hải Triều Âm. He said that on that day, on May 8th, 1963, he met with Cẩn before the incident. Cẩn said that he would call Saigon and he would rescind the order. But of course, that didn't happen, so I'm wondering if Thục overruled?

01:19:17PXA: Thục overruled. Because my cousin told me Thục overruled it.

01:19:21EM: And your cousin again is––

01:19:23PXA: Chief of Police and Security of Central Vietnam.

01:19:27EM: Lê Khắc Duyệt?

01:19:29PXA: Duyệt. D-U-Y-E-T.

01:19:31EM: Right, okay. And he was still the chief of security at that time?

01:19:35PXA: He was.

01:19:36EM: And he was a Buddhist?

01:19:37PXA: He Buddhist. Buddhist follower. He vegetarian too.

01:19:42EM: He told you that afterwards? He told you that Cẩn had been overruled?

01:19:48PXA: So the point in this is Ngô Đình Cẩn very smart. If Ngô Đình Nhu or Diệm listened to him, maybe the regime would last longer. Maybe, I'm not sure. Very difficult to tell for the mandarins, they can make a mistake by using them as the leader of the country. But after that, they keep to the Buddhists. The Buddhists don't know about politics. The Catholics know politics, but the Buddhists don't know it. So they need the Americans to teach them. So to clear all the file of Trí Quang working for French G2, the Americans ordered the Vietnamese to do it. But please don't publish this: Dr. Tuyến, he was asked by the chief of CIA, I think de Silva.

01:20:43EM: Who?

01:20:44PXA: de Silva. He's the chief CIA here.

01:20:49EM: Colby?

01:20:50PXA: No. Before Colby.

01:20:51EM: Before Colby?

01:20:52PXA: de Silva.

01:20:54EM: de Silva?

01:20:55PXA: Yeah. To take all the files and burn it.

01:21:01EM: Which files?

01:21:02PXA: The files left by the French G2 and the police, about Trí Quang and burn it, so no trace. Then he was sent to Cambodia as a representative of Buddhist at the meeting of the Buddhist unification.

01:21:23EM: Trí Quang would be sent?

01:21:26PXA: So Tuyến had a lot of enemies, he told me about that. But anyway, it's a secret. Even though he died, I don't want to know about that. Not to divulge this one, unless they agree to declassify, but I don't think the Americans would declassify.

01:21:45EM: Not yet.

01:21:46PXA: No, I don't think they would do it.

01:21:48EM: Right.

01:21:50PXA: But that's why some people want me to write a memo. I never––I don't want to do it, but this is for your knowledge.

01:21:58EM: I appreciate that very much because this is this is very useful to me because it helps me––

01:22:03PXA: The reason is I know the Buddhist will create hell, thanks to a CIA who was a professor in Huế. I'll tell you the name too– Mr. Jerry Rose. He worked for the Evening Star and the Washington Post, et cetera. He's a good friend of Stanley Karnow. Stanley, and he's my good friend too.

01:22:27EM: And he was CIA?

01:22:28PXA: He was––actually professor of English or something like that. He graduated from Sorbonne. He taught in Huế. He speaks Vietnamese a little bit, but not much. So because of the problem with adultery, particularly Mr. Barnes with the council in Huế, but his wife was involved with Jerry Rose. The man has a cold, you know––Mr. Barnes, the council, he had a cold blood. He found that, you know, flagrante deli[cto], but instead of pulling out a pistol and kill, he didn't do it. But he said, all right, you better go. And he left, he dared not stay in Huế, so he quit and he ran to Saigon.

01:23:26EM: So then he came to Saigon.

01:23:27PXA: He told me when he worked for a journalist at the Washington Post or Evening Post––Evening Star, something like that. He told me, Ẩn, you know a lot of people in Huế, you have to watch the Buddhists in the future, and you may have a scoop for Reuters. I did not know that was important, he told me about that in 1962.

01:23:53EM: So the CIA was already concerned about the Buddhists in Huế?

01:23:58PXA: They know about that! They know about that. They organize this kind of thing. Even they organized Trí Quang to go to the embassy too.

01:24:06EM: In '63?

01:24:08PXA: '63, yeah, when they revolted. [inaudible] follow the situation there, the Buddhists. [inaudible] All right, so I asked Mr. [inaudible] and my people over there to watch very closely for any sign unusual. Just call me from Huế. And maybe they call in 1963 about that, about Ngô Đình Thục, et cetera.

01:24:41EM: Before May, the signs were already there?

01:24:43PXA: And actually, I [inaudible], so I got the scoop for Reuters too. So Ngô Đình Cẩn is very smart, even at the courtroom. When Nguyễn Khánh sent him to the court, he was sentenced to death. He was sentenced to death at the military court, he and Dương Văn Hiếu––the one who worked for him and kidnapped all the communists and pro-communists in the south in Saigon here. They were sent to the military court because of illegal action; both of them carry [out] illegal action against civilians.

01:25:31EM: So when did this take place?

01:25:34PXA: In 1960. 1965––'64.

01:25:40EM: '64. This is when Cẩn has been captured?

01:25:43PXA: But that's after the coup. [inaudible] And Nguyễn Khánh overthrow the first junta, and then he sent them to the military court. The head of the military court, the judge, was Dương Hiếu Nghĩa, and the other one is Nguyễn Hoà Hiệp.

01:26:02EM: Nguyễn Hiếu Nghĩa? Was he––

01:26:09PXA: Colonel Dương Hiếu Nghĩa. He was Province Chief later in Vĩnh Long, et cetera. He's the Đại Việt leader. And Nguyễn Hoà Hiệp, the [Vietnamese?], he is Minister of Information. So, both of them sit there as the judge, with another one I forgot, but these two men were. So, they questioned him, and Ngô Đình Cẩn answered very well, very politely, fluently. One was "Thưa quý toà, tôi chỉ có là Cố vấn Phong trào Cách mạng Quốc gia thôi, tôi không có quyền gì hết. Nói là tôi bắt người này kia là không đúng." He was very smart, he denied everything, but the other one cannot. The other one asked for one thing: We capture one very important general, a VC general. You can sentence me to lie in prison, alright, but release me for a while so I can recapture that man, and then I will go back to jail.

01:27:12EM: Cẩn said this?

01:27:12PXA: No. Dương Văn Hiếu, the Chief of Secret Police in Central Vietnam. Actually, they decided life imprisonment for Dương Văn Hiếu–Chief of Secret Police in Central Vietnam. And Ngô Đình Cẩn sentenced to death. You know the reason why he was sentenced to death? He refused to return $2 million or $3 million in the bank in Switzerland to General Khánh. Instead, he gave it to the Catholic Church. That's why he deserved to be killed.

01:27:58EM: I see. So, if he had given the money then, Khánh would not have executed him?

01:28:04PXA: That's right. He would have been released. Trần Văn Đôn know about that.

01:28:13EM: Trần Văn Đôn? Oh! The general.

01:28:14PXA: Yeah, the one who pulled the coup. The one who planned the coup was Lê Văn Kim, his brother in law. To execute the coup, Trần Văn Đôn. Both of them are very good friends of [inaudible name] and Lou Conein. That's why these guys get together all the time. So I was there very often with them too. That's the reason why I know. But please write very carefully about that.
